new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Piapoco has an empty rule; Reinoso adds the type (a tonal accent system, accent on the nucleus, with morphophonemic shifts) but not the placement, since the deciding pages 60-64 are outside the open copy. Compatible with Klumpp 1985.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Reinoso classifies the suprasegmental system as 'acento-tonal' (a tonal accent): the accent sits on syllable nuclei, conditions consonant reinforcement (p. 42-43, 48: /p/, /t/, /θ/ are tense before a stressed vowel) and vowel half-lengthening (pp. 53-54: 'Se realiza alargada cuando está acentuada'). The placement rule and the tonal contrast are treated in 'El acento tonal' (pp. 60-64) and 'Cambios en el acento: en la posición del acento; de tonalidad' (pp. 79-80), which the open Rosetta excerpts do not include, so no placement rule can be quoted from this work.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not visible in the open excerpt; the contents list 'Afijos acentuales' (accented affixes, p. 62) and 'Eco acentual' (accentual echo, p. 64), which suggests multiple accents per word and accent-bearing affixes, consistent with Klumpp.
new_statements.exceptions: Contents list morphophonemic accent shifts ('En la posición del acento', p. 79) and tonal changes ('De tonalidad', p. 80); the open pages give none in detail.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog rule is empty; this is the fullest open statement: lexically placed, multiple, two-way (heavy/high vs lenis/low) stress. Data from Caño Cedro village (Vichada/Guaviare), fieldwork 1976-79 (n. 1, p. 27).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is lexical/morphemic, not positional: every stressed morpheme (stem or stressed affix) contributes one foot with a nuclear syllable; a simple word has one to four stressed syllables and any syllable can be stressed. There are two contrastive kinds of stress, 'heavy' (high pitch, tense voice) and 'lenis' (low pitch, husky voice), giving minimal pairs such as nucuaca 'I wait for' (lenis) vs nucuaca 'I toast' (heavy) and piini 'your breast' vs 'your urine' (p. 22). Klumpp explicitly labels this 'distinctive stress (contrastive phonetic exponents) as opposed to.. culminative stress (contrastive placement)' (pp. 26-27) and rejects the label pitch accent on terminological grounds while describing what the catalog list codes as pitch accent (lexically placed accent whose main exponent is pitch, with a H/L contrast). Vowel length is independent of stress (p. 22); clitics are unstressed (p. 20).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary-stress notion; instead multiple stresses per word (one to four nuclear syllables in a simple word, all heavy or all lenis; complex words such as nutanaacatena 'that I might write' mix heavy and lenis, p. 24). Unstressed marginal syllables have non-contrastive, fluctuating pitch (p. 22).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress perturbation at V+V morpheme boundaries: the stress moves to the first vowel of the resulting cluster and lenis stress takes precedence over heavy (p. 25, e.g. wa- + -aliacawa > waaliacawa). Words with only lenis stress give the impression of nearly equal stress on each syllable or of stress that shifts between repetitions, attributed to position in a higher-level unit (p. 24). Intermediate vowel length appears on the stressed syllable of disyllables in isolation (p. 23).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Klumpp gives no positional rule for stress: stress is a property of morphemes (stems and certain 'stressed affixes'), each stressed morpheme (+ clitics) forms a phonological foot, and a word may carry one to four stressed (nuclear) syllables; placement is lexical/morphological and 'must be determined by comparing the syllables of that word alone' (p. 24); examples show stress on first, second or third syllables (álitali, cawámai, cumàta, ibèeri, sumàu). On every stressed syllable there is a two-way lexical contrast, 'heavy' stress (= high pitch, tense voice) vs 'lenis' stress (= low pitch, husky voice, written with grave accent), with minimal pairs such as píini 'your urine' vs pìini 'your breast', úuwi 'battle' vs ùuwi 'her ear'; pitch is contrastive only on stressed syllables. Klumpp notes the system could be labelled word-tone or pitch accent ('distinctive stress' in Pilch's sense, contrastive exponents rather than contrastive placement) but keeps the term stress for Arawakanist reasons. Vowel length is independent of stress. Morphophonemic 'stress perturbation' moves stress to the first vowel of a V+V cluster at morpheme boundaries, lenis winning over heavy (p. 25). Rhythm is syllable-timed; unstressed vowels are not reduced.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No primary/secondary ranking is set up: a word has one stress per foot (one to four nuclear syllables), all described as full stresses of either the heavy or the lenis type; 'complex phonological words' mix heavy and lenis feet (p. 24). Unstressed (marginal) syllables have non-contrastive pitch. In all-lenis (low-pitch) words stress placement is hard to hear and may seem to shift between repetitions, which Klumpp attributes to phrase position (p. 24).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress perturbation rule V+V́ > V́V at morpheme boundaries with lenis taking precedence over heavy (sec. 2.2-2.3, p. 25); intermediate non-phonemic lengthening of the stressed vowel of disyllables in isolation (p. 23); interrogative phrases put a high rise on the final vowel (p. 26); /r/-initial words rare (one found).
new_statements.identity_note: Klumpp's data are from the village of Cano Cedro (rivers Vichada and Guaviare, eastern Colombia), fieldwork 1976-1979, using Sudo's (1976) practical orthography; no dialect differentiation is discussed.

readall_conflicts: No substantive disagreement. All three opened works describe the same system: stress is phonemic and lexically/morphemically placed, a word may carry one to four stresses, and each stressed syllable is either heavy (high pitch) or lenis (low pitch). The only difference is terminological: Klumpp 1985 deliberately calls the contrast 'heavy vs lenis distinctive stress' and rejects the label 'pitch accent' (p. 26), whereas Reinoso 2002 calls the suprasegmental system 'acento-tonal' (p. 39) and titles the section 'El acento tonal'. Both are what the fixed list codes as pitch accent; an alternative coding for the placement alone would be lexical (unpredictable), since Klumpp states 'any syllable is a unit of potential stress placement' and gives no positional rule. Reinoso's actual placement pages (60-64, 79-80) are not in the open excerpts, so no independent check of placement against Klumpp is possible.

Mosonyi agrees the accent is unpredictable (lexical) and that a word may carry more than one, but rejects the SIL two-quality (high-strong vs low-soft) analysis in favour of a si

sources.citation: Brend, Ruth M. (1985). From phonology to discourse: studies in six Colombian languages. SIL: LDAM 9. vi+133 pp.
sources.quote: p.20: 'Any syllable is a unit of potential stress placement.' p.21: 'The phonological word has one or more nuclear syllables bearing stress and potential pause at its final border. ... A simple phonological word has from one to four nuclear syllables, which bear either all heavy or all lenis stresses.' pp.21-22: 'A nuclear syllable with heavy stress carries a high pitch, while a nuclear syllable with lenis stress carries low pitch. The pitch of unstressed marginal syllables is noncontrastive and fluctuating ... in Piapoco, as in other "word-tone" languages, pitch is a significant feature of stressed syllables only.' p.26: 'for several reasons, the contrasts found in Piapoco have been called heavy and lenis stress rather than high and low pitch-accent.'
sources.locator: Klumpp 1985 in Brend (ed.) 1985, sec. 0.3 p. 20; sec. 1.1-1.1.2 pp. 21-22; sec. 1.1.6 p. 24; sec. 4 pp. 26-27 (pp. 26-28, 30, 32-33 of the full-volume scan)
sources.note: The catalog record for Piapoco has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so nothing is contradicted; this work supplies the first sourced description: lexically placed (morpheme-bound) stress, possibly multiple per word, with a contrastive heavy(high-pitch)/lenis(low-pitch) distinction on stressed syllables, i.e. a pitch accent/'word-tone'-like system in the author's own words. sources.citation: Klumpp, Deloris A. and Klumpp, James W. and Levinsohn, Stephen H. (1985). Piapoco: Continuity of situation and antitopic in narrative discourse. In From phonology to discourse: Studies in six Colombian languages. Dallas: Summer Institute of Linguistics. pp. 117-33.
sources.quote: "In addition, each word in Piapoco has one or more phonemes of stress. A word may have all heavy stresses or all lenis stresses or a combination of the two. Heavy stress is accompanied by high pitch on the stressed syllable and is indicated in the orthography by an acute accent: V́. Lenis stress is accompanied by low pitch and is indicated by the grave accent over the stressed vowel. V̀. For a description of the phonology of Piapoco, see Sudo 1976:7-14 and D. Klumpp's article in this volume."
sources.note: Agrees with Klumpp 1985 (work 1) and adds nothing beyond it; refines the empty catalog record in the same direction.

sources.citation: Klumpp, Deloris A. Pharris de. 1995. Vocabulario piapoco-español. Santafé de Bogotá: Asociación Instituto Lingüístico de Verano (Ed. Alberto Lleras Camargo). ix+190 pp. ISBN 978-958-21-0143-5. [front matter 'Notas ortográficas'; appendix 'Bosquejo gramatical']
sources.quote: Cada palabra en piapoco tiene uno o mis [más] acentos. El acento fuerte se representa con una tilde aguda ( ' ) sobre la vocal acentuada y va acompaflada [acompañada] por un tono alto; el acento ctebil [débil] se representa con una tilde grave ( ' ) sobre de la vocal acentuada y va acompaflada [acompañada] por un tono bajo. (scanned text layer, bracketed readings mine) | Bosquejo gramatical, n. 4: La tilde encima del guidn [guión] indica que la silaba anterior I leva [lleva] tono alto.
sources.locator: 'Notas ortográficas', and 'Bosquejo gramatical' footnote 4 + prefixation section
sources.note: First-hand orthographic/prosodic note: every Piapoco word carries one or more accents; two accent types are distinguished and written throughout the dictionary — 'acento fuerte' (acute) accompanied by HIGH tone and 'acento débil' (grave) accompanied by LOW tone; the grammar sketch adds that prefixation can shift the accent from root to prefix (pi-aliawa > pialiawa, wa-uca > wòucà) and marks high tone on preceding syllables in morpheme glossing (fn. 4). I.e. the whole lexicon is tone/accent-marked under the Klumpp heavy(high)/lenis(low) stress analysis.

The strong accent is written with an acute accent mark over the accented vowel and is accompanied by a high tone; the weak accent is written with a grave accent mark over the accented vowel and is accompanied by a low tone. | Grammar sketch, n. 4: The accent mark over the hyphen indicates that the preceding syllable bears high tone.
